claims.text: The initial equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase FCC solid solution with a random atomic distribution.
The initial crystal contains no pre-existing vacancy clusters or HCP phases.
Low-temperature conditions minimize atomic thermal vibrations.
The relevant deformation regime spans strain rates from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Temperatures from 100 K to 300 K suppress thermally activated cross-slip while still permitting dislocation nucleation.
Single-crystal geometry isolates crystallographic-orientation effects on yielding.
Plastic deformation is mediated by Shockley partial dislocations with Burgers vectors of the 1/6<112> type.
Shockley partials nucleate at ordinary lattice sites or pre-existing defects.
Shockley partials create intrinsic stacking faults on {111} planes.
The partial-dislocation density and intrinsic-stacking-fault width vary with loading orientation.
Yielding is governed by the critical resolved shear stress needed to nucleate Shockley partials on favorably oriented {111} slip planes.
The <11-1> loading orientation maximizes the Schmid factor for the primary Shockley-partial slip systems.
The <11-1> orientation has a higher maximum yield stress than the <110> orientation.
The reduced resolved shear stress on primary {111}<112> systems under <110> loading causes that orientation to yield at a lower applied stress.
HCP-like faulted regions have an interplanar spacing of 0.123 nm, compared with 0.124 nm for HCP.
The HCP-like regions lack the long-range order characteristic of a true phase.
Stacking faults can be distinguished from a true HCP phase by HRTEM lattice-fringe analysis combined with diffraction analysis.
Diffraction streaking indicates stacking faults, whereas discrete HCP diffraction spots indicate a true phase transformation.
Under the stated regime, twinning and FCC-to-BCC transformations are suppressed.
The deformed regions should exhibit intrinsic stacking faults without distinct HCP diffraction spots or significant lattice-parameter shifts.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says <11-1> maximizes the Schmid factor yet requires a higher applied stress to reach the nucleation threshold, while <110> has a reduced resolved-shear component yet yields at a lower applied stress. Under the stated CRSS-controlled mechanism, these geometric premises imply the opposite applied-stress ordering, so the proposed mechanism does not coherently produce the predicted orientation dependence.

The initial state excludes pre-existing vacancy clusters, but the mediator allows nucleation at pre-existing defects and the uncertainty discusses the critical stress for nucleation at vacancy clusters. The hypothesis therefore does not specify whether vacancy-cluster nucleation is part of the tested system.
